intro: If you're a UK national living abroad and you've searched for the best expat mortgage near me, you're probably trying to buy or remortgage UK property from overseas. You want a mortgage broker who understands expat lending and can introduce you to a suitable professional. iComply is a free introduction service — you tell us what you need and we introduce you to a UK mortgage broker who quotes you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for an expat mortgage usually need
need_lead: Expat mortgages are a niche area, and the right broker can make the process much smoother.
needs: You live outside the UK but want to buy a UK home to live in later or rent out.
You already own a UK property and need to remortgage from abroad, perhaps to a better rate.
Your income is in a foreign currency and you need a broker who understands how lenders assess that.
You have a larger deposit than a typical UK buyer and want to know how that affects your options.
You've been turned down by high street lenders because you live overseas and need specialist help.
context_heading: Why 'best' and 'near me' need a closer look for expat mortgages
context: Searching for the best expat mortgage near me can be misleading because 'best' depends on your circumstances — your income currency, deposit size and whether the property is for you or for rent. Rather than looking for a label, ask brokers how they search the market and whether they have experience with expat cases like yours. 'Near me' matters less for expat mortgages because most advice is handled remotely, so you can work with a broker anywhere in the UK.

Mortgage advice is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Any broker or adviser you use should be authorised, or be an appointed representative of an authorised firm, and you can check this on the FCA register. Advisers typically hold a qualification such as CeMAP. Brokers must tell you whether they search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders, and how they are paid, whether by lender commission, a fee, or both.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Where you currently live and your nationality, as expat lending often depends on residency and citizenship.
Whether you are buying a new UK property or remortgaging an existing one.
The currency your income is paid in and whether it is a salary, pension or other regular income.
How much deposit you have available, or how much equity you hold if remortgaging.
Whether the property will be your main home, a second home or a buy-to-let investment.
Any timeline you have in mind, such as a property purchase deadline or a remortgage end date.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the mortgage broker
questions: Do you have experience arranging mortgages for UK nationals living abroad?
Do you search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders for expat mortgages?
How do you assess foreign currency income when working out what I can borrow?
What deposit size do lenders typically look for from expat borrowers?
How are you paid for your work — by lender commission, a fee, or both?
Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and can you provide your firm's reference number?

faqs.q: Can I get a UK mortgage if I live abroad?
faqs.a: Yes, but fewer lenders offer expat deals. A broker who specialises in expat mortgages can tell you which lenders are likely to consider your situation.

faqs.q: Does my foreign income count for a UK mortgage?
faqs.a: Lenders that accept expat applications will assess your foreign currency income, often converting it to sterling. The amount you can borrow will depend on the lender's criteria and the currency involved.

faqs.q: Will I need a bigger deposit as an expat?
faqs.a: Larger deposits are common for expat mortgages, as lenders see overseas borrowers as higher risk. A broker can explain what deposit size lenders typically expect for your circumstances.

faqs.q: How do I check a mortgage broker is authorised?
faqs.a: You can check on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) register. Brokers must be authorised or be an appointed representative of an authorised firm, and they should tell you how they are paid.

extra_heading: What happens after you're introduced to a broker
extra: Once iComply introduces you to a mortgage broker, the first conversation usually focuses on your residency, nationality and the currency your income is paid in. The broker will need to understand whether you're buying a new UK property or remortgaging an existing one, and whether it will be your home or a buy-to-let. This helps them identify which lenders on their panel might consider your case.

You'll likely be asked for documents such as proof of identity, proof of address overseas, evidence of income (such as payslips or pension statements) and bank statements. Because expat lending often involves foreign currency, the broker may also discuss how lenders convert your income to sterling and what deposit size they typically expect. They should explain their advice process and any fees before you proceed.

The broker will then research suitable lenders and recommend a mortgage that fits your circumstances. They must tell you whether they search the whole of the market or a limited panel, and how they are paid. If you have any concerns, you can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

extra_faqs.q: Will I need to travel to the UK to meet my mortgage broker?
extra_faqs.a: Most expat mortgage advice is handled remotely by phone, email or video call, so you usually won't need to travel. The broker will let you know if any documents need to be signed in person or witnessed.

extra_faqs.q: Can I use a broker near my overseas home?
extra_faqs.a: Mortgage brokers who arrange UK mortgages for expats can be based anywhere in the UK and still help you. What matters is their experience with expat lending and that they are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), which you can check on the FCA register.
